**Proof.**

Yes, the condition implies $f(x) \equiv 0$ on $[a,b]$.

Since the hypothesis holds for *every* continuous function $g$ on $[a,b]$, we are free to choose a particular $g$. Set

$$g(x) = f(x).$$

Because $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, this $g$ is itself a continuous function on $[a,b]$, so the hypothesis applies, giving

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,g(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx = 0.$$

Now $f$ is continuous, so $f^2$ is continuous, and

$$f(x)^2 \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in [a,b].$$

A continuous, non-negative function whose integral over $[a,b]$ is zero must vanish identically. Indeed, suppose for contradiction that $f(x_0)^2 > 0$ at some $x_0 \in [a,b]$. By continuity, there exists an interval $I \subseteq [a,b]$ of positive length containing $x_0$ on which $f(x)^2 \geq \tfrac{1}{2}f(x_0)^2 > 0$. Then

$$\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx \geq \int_I f(x)^2\,dx \geq \tfrac{1}{2}f(x_0)^2 \cdot |I| > 0,$$

contradicting $\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx = 0$.

Therefore $f(x)^2 \equiv 0$ on $[a,b]$, hence $f(x) \equiv 0$ on $[a,b]$. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
